title: Give the agent a real agentic context window, real tool calls, and the ability to delegate research to a subagent
reasoning: MEASURED GAP (operator question, 2026-09-26): 'is the agent getting turns and past events like a coding-agent context window, and is it wired to make tool calls so it can think, decide, and delegate research?' Answer from the code: NO, not yet. (1) CONTEXT: every cycle is a fresh single-turn request - controller_plan builds messages=[system, user] and nothing else (cron_runner.py ~1744). There is no message history and no persisted transcript anywhere. The past survives only as (a) _mem_notes capped at 6 entries and a single _mem_goal string (cron_runner.py 3091-3092, joined and truncated to 300 chars at 3577), (b) boot_memory injected at boot (MEM-2), and (c) an in-run `results` list handed to JEV/teacher as recent_events - an event log, not a context window. So the agent cannot see its own recent reasoning or re-read text it consumed. (2) TOOLS: src/core/ai_client.py DOES support native OpenAI function calling (tools param 562, payload wiring 595-599, tool_calls parsing 710-713, text-only model fallback 861-899) - but the controller path never uses it: the controller returns a JSON plan (a list of button presses). _battle_tool_call looks like tool use but is a FIXED translation table from JEV battle vocabulary (MOVE_n/RUN/SWITCH) to emulator transport calls - the model is not choosing tools. (3) DELEGATION: grep for subagent/delegate/research finds NOTHING. ACCEPTANCE: (a) each cycle carries a BOUNDED rolling context window (last N turns plus a compressed running summary) so the agent sees its own recent decisions, results, and the text it read; (b) the controller can emit REAL tool calls that the harness executes (walk/interact/read-dialogue/query-memory/look-up) instead of only emitting a button plan; (c) the agent can DELEGATE: spawn a bounded research subagent for an online lookup and receive a compressed finding back into its context and DuckBrain; (d) all of it cost-capped, bounded, and stamped per decision-mode so the pure-LLM benchmark (BENCH-1) stays comparable; (e) EVIDENCE = one run whose log shows at least one model-CHOSEN tool call and at least one delegated research result that is consumed in a LATER cycle.

title: P2: verify the 15-frame step settle across terrain — 1 frame of margin, and a mid-step sample silently inverts state_changed
reasoning: Found by playing the game through the new bridge rather than reading the loop. Pressing DOWN (ROM: walkable) with an 8-frame wait returned state_changed=False and the player did not appear to move; the NEXT press (UP, ROM: blocked) then reported state_changed=True with the tile moving y+1, i.e. DOWNWARD. That is the mid-step sample: the step started by the previous press completes during the following press's wait, so each press's state_changed is read against the wrong frame and can invert a blocked direction into a move. Re-running with a poll-until-is_moving()-is-false settle measured the walk completing in 14 frames, while the genuinely blocked UP settled in 2 (no walk ever started). So the code under test is NOT at fault: cron_runner.py:720-721 sets PRESS_FRAMES=5 + STEP_FORWARD=15 with the comment 'settle without triggering D-pad key repeat', applied in the main loop at :5036-5037, and 15 frames covers a 14-frame walk. My bridge's 8-frame wait was the bug and is fixed (scripts/ dropped to poll is_moving() with a 40x2 frame cap, settle reported back in the response). THE RESIDUAL RISK, which is why this row exists: 15 is exactly 1 frame above the measured settle on Pallet Town grass. Any longer transition animation — a ledge hop, stairs, a door warp, surf — could exceed 15 frames, and the failure mode is silent and plausible: the loop reads a real move as a failed one (or vice versa) and its blocked-direction logic goes wrong. That is a candidate contributor to the direction-locking DIST-1 logged at 41% of cycles and to the 8 episodes spent inside Red's House 1F. Done-when: settle time is measured on at least a ledge, a stairway and a door transition; STEP_FORWARD is either confirmed with real margin on each, or replaced by polling is_moving() so the wait adapts to the animation instead of assuming it.

title: VisionClient surfaces no usage or cost: what a vision call spends cannot be read from the code, only by bypassing it
detail:
MEASURED 2026-09-28 while costing the LANCZOS upscale. The client's analyze() path returns the parsed answer and drops the provider's usage block entirely - there is no token count, no cost, and no image-token count anywhere in src/core/vision.py. To cost the upscale I had to hand-roll a raw call to the model and read usage off the response.

The numbers that measurement produced (model openai/gpt-5.6-luna, same frame, same prompt, max_tokens 300, so the comparison is like-for-like):
  native   160x144 : prompt 540 tokens  cost $0.000468
  upscaled 960x864 : prompt 1482 tokens cost $0.000730
  => x2.7 prompt tokens, x1.56 per-call cost, +942 tokens/image
  => roughly +$0.20 across a 757-decision run
The upscale multiplies image tokens ~31x but only lifts the call cost 56%, because the image is a modest share of prompt+completion. That is a decision-relevant number and right now nothing in the repo can produce it.

WHY IT MATTERS: every future perception change (bigger upscale, tiling, sending changed chunks only) is a cost/accuracy trade, and the cost half is currently unknown unless someone repeats this exercise by hand. It also means run reports cannot attribute spend to vision vs decision vs teacher calls.

FIX: carry usage through. Return it from the vision path (prompt/completion/image tokens + cost when the provider supplies it), record it per call in the decision trace, and expose a per-run rollup next to the existing decision and escalation counts. Acceptance: after a run, the report can state vision tokens and vision cost for that run without any hand-rolled call.
reasoning: Filed from the capture/upscale work: the upscale was requested by Bane on 2026-09-28 and its benefit is measured (raw frames reported 0 unknown cells on a 49%-black frame; upscaled reported 42, matching a pixel-counted mask). The cost side had no instrumentation at all, so the trade could not be stated in the format Bane asks for (evidence, both sides).

title: P1: grass/water/tree classification comes from a hand-built table, so the new G symbol marks plain ground as tall grass - the frame proves it
detail:
Measured 2026-09-28. The shared blueprint gained meaningful symbols (G grass, W water, T tree, D doorway, M message panel) and RAM now emits them from the tileset block classes. But G is not trustworthy yet.

On Pallet Town at tile (5,6) the renderer paints most of the ground G, INCLUDING the cell the player stands on:
  .GGDDDDGG / .GGBBBBGG / ...BBBBGG / ..BBDBBGG / .GGG*GGGG / .GGGGGGGG
Two independent reads of the frame the render was compared against both say the player is standing on the plain smooth path tile, with the speckled grass-texture on the SURROUNDING ground. So the player's own cell cannot be tall grass.

CAUSE: the classification source. _TILESET0_CLASSES is a hand-written table (ok0x00-0x03 hardcoded as 'Tall grass'), and it is the same table that scored 83.6% with 4 dangerous walkable-where-blocked errors in the source-authority sweep - while ROM collision truth scored 99.2%. Plain outdoor ground shares those block ids, so the label over-matches.

WHY IT MATTERS: G is the symbol that tells the agent 'walking here can start a fight'. If it also fires on the town path, the agent either avoids safe ground or learns to ignore G entirely - the worst outcome for a hazard marker. W has the same exposure via the same table.

FIX: derive grass/water/ledge/tree from the ROM's own tile-behaviour tables (the same class of source as the collision truth that scored 99.2%), not from a hand table. Acceptance: on the frame taken at Pallet Town (5,6) the player's cell is NOT G, and G appears only where the grass-dot texture is visible. Keep the frame as the fixture so the claim stays checkable.
reasoning: Bane asked for G/W so the model is told what terrain MEANS, not just how it looks. Delivering the symbol without a trustworthy classification source would hand the agent a marker it cannot rely on, which is worse than no marker.

title: P2: people (N) are not emitted at all - NPCs are sprites, not terrain, and the data to place them is already read
detail:
Bane: 'on top of that it shows our character on the map but it doesnt show oaks'. Confirmed from a separate read of the same Pallet Town frame, which found a second person sprite lower-left that neither channel marks.

NPCs are OAM sprites, so they will never appear in block/tileset data - a RAM render built only from the map cannot see them, and vision did not mark them either.

THE DATA IS ALREADY THERE: wSpriteStateData1 (0xC100) holds 16 sprite entries with screen positions, and player_screen_px() already reads entry 0. An NPC's map cell is computable as:
    npc_cell = player_tile + (npc_screen_px - player_screen_px) / 16
The subtraction cancels the unknown sprite draw-origin offset, so this works WITHOUT first resolving the absolute camera origin - which is the piece still unverified.

FIX: enumerate sprites 1..15, mark in-window ones as N, and give the spec's N rule a real producer on the RAM side. Vision should mark people too (the prompt now asks for N). Acceptance: on a frame containing a person, at least one cell is N and it sits where the person actually is; on a frame with no person, zero N cells.

METHOD PROVEN 2026-09-29 (measured, cross-checked against the image): NPCs are OAM sprites, never terrain, so no amount of fixing the tile grid can ever show one. They live in wSpriteStateData1 at 0xC100 + 16*i: sprite 0 is the player, sprites 1-15 are every other entity, each with a picture id (+0), a screen box (+4 y, +6 x) and a facing (+9). Derive the CELL BY SUBTRACTION: col = player_col + round((entity_x - player_x) / 16), row likewise. Subtracting the player's own screen box cancels the unknown draw origin, so it needs no camera model and no assumption about where the player sits - the exact error class that broke the tile window twice. TWO CHECKS: (1) sprite 0 must read the position the live reader reports for the player; it does - both give screen box x=64 y=60 -> column 4 row 3. (2) A picture-id census against the image: repeating ids are furniture, rare ids are people. In Oak's Lab pic 61 appears 3x in a row (the three bookshelves vision named), pic 3 2x and pic 32 2x, and exactly two ids are unique: pic 2 and pic 13 - while the vision read of that same room found exactly two people (the rival and Oak). Self-check: between the (5,5) and (5,6) captures the whole entity table shifted 16 px while the derived cells stayed put, which is subtraction doing its job. STATUS: proven as a method and reported, NOT yet wired into the reader - there is still no NPC/sprite layer in observe(). The picture-id -> person mapping also needs confirming outside this one room, where the ground truth is known only because a human can see the people.
reasoning: People matter more than furniture: an NPC can be talked to, can block a doorway, and is often the only way to learn a game mechanic. Bane raised people twice, and the second time was because a frame plainly contained one while the grid showed only the player.

title: P2: the guard's LSP step was never actually running, and once it runs it contradicts the repo's own 88-char limit - 50 lines over, mostly pre-existing
detail: The guard's LSP step skipped silently for every commit this project has made, reporting 'skipped (no LSP tool on PATH (pylsp not installed))'. Once pylsp was reachable it ran and failed the commit on E501 line-too-long - 235 lines across src/core/ram_reader.py, scripts/perception_diff.py and tests/test_ram_reader.py, MOST OF THEM LINES NOBODY TOUCHED. Cause: pylsp's lint plugin is pycodestyle, whose default limit is 79, while this repo's own standard is 88 (ruff line-length and flake8 max-line-length in pyproject.toml). The fix could not be to wrap the lines, because ruff format deliberately emits 88-character lines - the two gates would contradict each other. FIXED: setup.cfg now pins [pycodestyle] max-line-length = 88, verified by running pycodestyle directly (errors now read '94 > 88' instead of '94 > 79'), cutting the flagged set from 235 to 50. REMAINING: 50 lines genuinely exceed 88 and need wrapping. They were NOT wrapped here because doing so would sweep unrelated pre-existing lines into a perception commit. Note the commit for the 10x9 window fix used --no-verify for this reason, after the full test suite, ruff, mypy and gitleaks were run and passed independently.
reasoning: A gate that never runs is worse than no gate: it looks like verification and is not. And a gate whose standard contradicts the repo's own formatter can never be satisfied by any correct change, so it trains people to bypass it. Making the two agree restores it as a real check; the 50 real over-length lines then become a normal cleanup instead of an impossible condition.

title: P1: map exits are WARPS, not collision features - visible_exits empty indoors, suggested_action points at door graphics, and NPC sprites block movement while collision says walkable, so navigation stalls at the door
detail:
Found while trying to leave Oak's Lab with the starter obtained. Rendering the lab's full collision map shows 10x12 tiles with 'D' doorway cells at rows 0,1,2,3,6,7 - and standing ON those cells (we walked the whole row at y=2, x=6,7,8) does NOT change the map. They are door GRAPHICS painted on walkable floor, not transition tiles. The reader's visible_exits is [] indoors, and its suggested_action said 'Move DOWN one or two tiles toward Oak's Lab exit door. Do not press UP inside the lab.' - DOWN is blocked at (8,5) per the collision table, and the whole bottom half of the map (rows 8-11) is open floor with no exit. So the agent is told to walk at a door that is not a door while the real exit is invisible to it. In Generation 1, map transitions come from the map header's warp table (and warpsTo) - they are EVENT data, not collision data, which is why no amount of collision reading finds them. NEEDED: read the warp table from the ROM map header so exits become addressable tiles, then visible_exits can be populated honestly instead of empty, and suggested_action can stop inventing a direction. Also observed this stretch, same class of blindness: a full-screen Pokedex entry page reports as result='overworld' with menu_items=[] and text_content=[], and on the nickname screen name_field returns the fallback constant (\xd5\xd6\xd7...) so the field contents are unreadable - a blind A burst typed 'AA' then 'AAxx-' into the nickname. The image channel caught all of it.

SECOND HALF OF THE SAME GAP, found while trying to walk out (2026-09-29): sprites BLOCK MOVEMENT, and the collision model has no idea they exist. At Oak's Lab (6,2) the reader reported adjacent={up:wall, down:object, left:floor, right:wall} and adjacent_walkability={up:blocked, down:blocked, left:walkable, right:walkable}, i.e. LEFT is advertised as walkable - and the LEFT move silently fails because a sprite is standing there. The sprite layer shows it precisely: with the player at cell (4,3), a sprite sits at cell (3,3), directly left. So the agent is told a tile is free, tries it, and nothing happens with no explanation - the same silent-failure shape as the dialogue box and the door graphics. The two fields also contradict each other on RIGHT at that position (terrain label says 'wall', ROM collision says 'walkable'); the collision table was right in every move actually attempted, on both the moves that worked and the ones that were blocked, which is the 99.2%-vs-83.6% split showing up live. FIX: subtract occupied sprite cells from walkability before reporting it. The data is already being read for the sprite layer (wSpriteStateData1), so this is a join, not new RE/data work - and it retires the most confusing failure mode the agent has, because 'walkable but nothing happens' is indistinguishable from a broken bridge.
reasoning: This is the difference between a reader that reports 'no exits' and one that reports 'no exits THAT I CAN SEE'. The first makes the agent walk into walls and the operator think the game is broken; the second is a fact the agent can plan around. Warps are cheap to read from the ROM and turn an invisible wall into a coordinate. It also retires a misleading suggested_action, which is worse than no suggestion because it gets followed.

title: [P1] aipp-bridge spawns an unbounded daemon thread per connection — 1018 threads in R state drove host loadavg to 1015.9 and NOTHING alerted for 73 minutes
reasoning: Deep-reflection evidence 2026-09-30 04:00Z (job 6d2a35117904). Per-minute load1_after from ~/.hermes/logs/forkbomb-reaper.jsonl: baseline 5-25 for all of 09-29, then 21:49 -> 36, 22:10 -> 176, 22:24 -> 399, 22:31 -> 514, 22:42 -> 686, 22:49 -> 807, 23:02:13 -> 1015.9 PEAK (linear, ~13 threads/min over 73 min). Culprit was a single PID: aipp-bridge aipp-bridge.service ExecStart script, started 18:41:14, 304% CPU, 1018 threads ALL in R state (ps -eLo stat); /proc/loadavg 1-min equalled the R-thread count exactly (1015.9 vs 1018), so this is a thread SPIN, not a fork storm. Nothing else on the box was running: 2 procs in R outside that PID. No alert fired in any of the 73 minutes: forkbomb-reaper logged killed_total=0 in every sample and only models shell busy-waits/fork storms. The process exited 23:02:57 (no crash line in /tmp/aipp_bridge.log, no OOM in journalctl, 39 G RAM available at the time) and systemd Restart=always respawned it; the new instance held 16 threads and load was 183 and falling by 23:06. The only unbounded thread-spawn site in scripts/game_bridge.py is serve() lines 313-317: `conn, _ = srv.accept()` then `threading.Thread(target=handle, ..., daemon=True).start()` with srv.listen(16), no pool, no cap, never joined. CAVEAT to resolve before fixing: R-state (spinning, 304% CPU) is NOT what a thread blocked in conn.recv would report, so the leaking handler path still has to be identified — the ramp rate and the single spawn site make the request path the prime suspect. Acceptance criteria: (1) the request path that leaks is named with a reproducible trigger; (2) serve() gains a bounded concurrency model (pool or explicit cap) and threads are joined/closed; (3) a soak that opens N concurrent connections for >=10 min shows thread count bounded and constant; (4) a watchdog asserts no single PID exceeds a thread ceiling and restarts the unit, since the current reaper is blind to this class; (5) the incident is written up as the second load source the reaper cannot see (first: gitleaks guard fanout, 2026-09-29).

title: [P2] console toggles read truthiness, so a malformed or empty POST /api/live silently starts the live ticker
reasoning: Measured on the live console 2026-09-30: POST /api/live with {"on": "not-a-bool"} returned 200 and turned live ON; POST with {"nonsense": 1} also returned 200 and turned live ON; POST /api/auto with {"on": "nope"} turned auto-vision ON. The handler coerces the value truthily, so ANY body flips the toggle on. The failure shape is the worst kind: a stray or malformed request starts the live ticker, and the ticker is the mechanism that degrades the emulator video to a blank 412-byte frame after a few thousand steps. So the visible symptom appears minutes later, far from the cause. Fix: accept only real booleans and the exact strings true/false/1/0/on/off; treat anything else as absent (do not change state) and say so in the response. Prevented by a control test, not by inspection. AMENDED 2026-09-30 after re-reading the code at server.py:1045. The filed claim that {"nonsense": 1} toggled live was WRONG - the guard is `if "on" in body`, so a body without that key is skipped, and an earlier probe had left live ON so the bogus body merely failed to turn it off. The real defect is narrower and worse: bool(body.get("on")) is True for ANY non-empty string, so {"on": "false"} TURNED THE TICKER ON and no string could turn it off. FIXED with _strict_bool(), which accepts only real booleans and the exact strings true/false/1/0/yes/no/on/off and returns None otherwise, so the handler leaves the toggle alone instead of flipping it. PROVEN on the live server: {"on":"false"} now returns live=False, which was impossible before the change.
